gloss_terse: To remain beside, continue with, abide; to stay on in a place or role, persevere steadfastly.
gloss_readable: Derived from para (beside) and meno (remain), this verb carries the sense of staying alongside someone or something with loyal persistence. In Philippians 1:25, Paul uses it for his confident expectation of continuing with the believers for their progress in the faith. James 1:25 applies it to the one who 'continues' gazing into the perfect law — not a passing glance but a settled, abiding attentiveness. The multilingual evidence consistently renders it with words for 'remain' (Spanish permanecer, German bleiben, French demeurer), underscoring the theme of faithful, enduring presence.

senses.1: To remain with, continue alongside, persevere in a relationship, place, or commitment. The translations across languages — Spanish continuaré/permanecer, German bleiben, French demeurer — all converge on loyal, ongoing presence. Paul uses it of staying alive for the churches' benefit (Phil 1:25), while Hebrews 7:23 contrasts mortal priests who cannot 'continue' with Christ's permanent priesthood. James 1:25 extends the image to abiding engagement with God's word.

gloss_terse: To encourage, console, comfort; to speak words of reassurance or exhortation to those in distress.
gloss_readable: This verb blends encouragement with tender consolation. At the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:19, 31), Jewish mourners come to 'comfort' Martha and Mary — the Greek captures the warmth of personal presence in grief. Paul employs it in 1 Thessalonians 2:12 for the way a father encourages his children, and in 5:14 for comforting the fainthearted. Spanish consolad/consolando and German troesten highlight the consolation axis, while English 'encourage' captures the forward-looking, hope-giving dimension.

senses.1: To comfort, console, and encourage — especially by coming alongside someone in grief or discouragement and offering reassuring, strengthening words. The multilingual evidence (Spanish consolad, German troesten, French consoler) clusters around deep emotional comfort. John 11:19 and 11:31 show this in the context of mourning Lazarus, while 1 Thessalonians 2:12 and 5:14 reveal the pastoral side: exhorting believers toward faithfulness and heartening the discouraged.

gloss_terse: To prepare, make ready, equip; to arrange in advance for an anticipated event or need.
gloss_readable: Built from para (alongside, in advance) and skeuazo (equip), this verb emphasizes deliberate, purposeful readiness. In Acts 10:10, a meal is 'being prepared' when Peter receives his vision on the rooftop — mundane preparation becomes the stage for divine revelation. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 9:2-3 for the Corinthians' financial readiness, and in 1 Corinthians 14:8 for a trumpet giving a clear sound so soldiers can 'prepare' for battle. Every major translation language echoes the same core: Spanish preparar, German vorbereiten, French préparer.

senses.1: To prepare, make ready, or equip in advance for a coming event, action, or need. All translation traditions converge — Spanish preparar, German vorbereiten, French préparer — on the sense of purposeful, advance arrangement. Acts 10:10 uses it of a meal being prepared, 1 Corinthians 14:8 of battle readiness signaled by a trumpet, and 2 Corinthians 9:2-3 of the Corinthians' generous financial readiness that Paul boasts about to the Macedonians.

gloss_terse: To carry aside, remove; to be swept along or carried away by force, influence, or deception.
gloss_readable: From para (aside, past) and phero (carry), this verb evokes powerful movement that sweeps something off course. In the Gethsemane prayers (Mark 14:36; Luke 22:42), Jesus asks the Father to 'remove' the cup of suffering — a deeply personal plea. Hebrews 13:9 warns against being 'carried away' by diverse and strange teachings, while Jude 12 paints false teachers as waterless clouds 'carried along' by winds. The Spanish translations split revealingly between quita/pasa (remove/pass) and llevadas (carried away), mirroring the verb's dual force: active removal and passive drift.

senses.1: To carry aside, remove, or sweep away — either by deliberate action (removal of something unwanted) or by external force (being carried off course). Mark 14:36 and Luke 22:42 use it in Jesus' prayer to remove the cup, showing volitional removal. Hebrews 13:9 and Jude 1:12 shift to the passive: being carried away by false teachings or blown about like empty clouds. The multilingual evidence — German fortreissen (tear away), Spanish llevadas (carried), French emporter (carry off) — captures this dynamic force.

gloss_terse: To spend the winter, overwinter; to stay at a location through the cold season.
gloss_readable: A practical, seasonal verb combining para (at, beside) and cheima (winter), referring to remaining in a place during the winter months when sea travel was dangerous. Ancient Mediterranean navigation shut down roughly from November to March, making winter quarters a strategic necessity. In Acts 27:12, the sailors debate wintering at a suitable harbor in Crete. Acts 28:11 notes Paul's departure from Malta on a ship that had 'wintered' there. Paul himself plans to winter with the Corinthians (1 Cor 16:6) and asks Titus to meet him at Nicopolis where he intends to winter (Titus 3:12).

senses.1: To spend the winter season at a particular location, typically because sea travel was impossible or perilous during cold months. Every translation tradition uses a seasonally specific word — Spanish invernar, German ueberwintern, French hiverner — rather than a generic 'stay.' Acts 27:12 captures the nautical urgency of finding a safe harbor before winter storms, while 1 Corinthians 16:6 and Titus 3:12 show Paul using winter stays for extended fellowship and ministry planning.

gloss_terse: A sojourner, resident alien, foreigner; one who dwells in a land not their own without full citizenship.
gloss_readable: This adjective-turned-noun (from para, beside, and oikos, house) describes someone living alongside but not truly belonging to a community — a resident alien. Stephen's speech recalls how Abraham's descendants were 'sojourners' in Egypt (Acts 7:6), and Moses became a sojourner in Midian (Acts 7:29). Ephesians 2:19 dramatically reverses the status: Gentile believers are 'no longer strangers and sojourners' but fellow citizens with God's people. First Peter 2:11 reclaims the term positively, urging Christians to live as 'sojourners and exiles' in this world, reorienting their ultimate belonging to heaven.

senses.1: A sojourner, resident alien, or stranger dwelling in a foreign land without full rights of citizenship. Spanish extranjero/forastero and German Fremdling both emphasize foreignness, while the Greek root para + oikos (beside the house) evokes living on the margins of a household. Acts 7:6 and 7:29 use it historically of Israel in Egypt and Moses in Midian. Ephesians 2:19 transforms it theologically — believers are no longer paroikoi — and 1 Peter 2:11 embraces it as the Christian's proper stance toward the present world.

gloss_terse: Patriarch; the founding father or chief ancestor of a family, tribe, or nation.
gloss_readable: Composed of patria (family line) and arche (beginning, rule), this title designates the founding ancestors of Israel. In Acts 2:29, Peter calls David a 'patriarch,' elevating him alongside the ancestral fathers. Acts 7:8-9 applies it to Jacob's twelve sons — the patriarchs of Israel's tribes — noting their jealousy toward Joseph. Hebrews 7:4 uses it of Abraham in his encounter with Melchizedek, emphasizing Abraham's exalted status to heighten how remarkable it is that he paid tithes to a priestly figure outside his own line. Every language renders it with a recognizable cognate: Spanish patriarca, French patriarche, German Erzvaeter.

senses.1: A patriarch — the founding father or chief progenitor of a family line, tribe, or nation, especially one of Israel's revered ancestors. The term carries both genealogical and spiritual authority. Acts 2:29 applies it to David, Acts 7:8-9 to the twelve sons of Jacob, and Hebrews 7:4 to Abraham. The cross-linguistic consistency (Spanish patriarca, French patriarche, German Erzvaeter) reflects the word's universal recognition as a title of ancestral honor and leadership.

gloss_terse: To obey one in authority, submit to a ruler or authoritative command; comply with direction.
gloss_readable: Built from peitho (persuade, trust) and arche (authority, rule), this verb denotes obedience directed specifically toward those in positions of authority — whether divine or civil. The dramatic declaration in Acts 5:29, 'We must obey God rather than men,' uses this word to set divine authority above human, making it a landmark text on conscience and civil disobedience. Acts 5:32 links obedience to receiving the Holy Spirit. Acts 27:21 applies it practically — the sailors should have 'obeyed' Paul's nautical advice. Titus 3:1 calls believers to be ready to obey rulers and authorities.

senses.1: To obey or submit to those in authority — a structured, authority-directed obedience rather than mere compliance. Spanish obedecer, German gehorchen, and French obéir all capture this official dimension. Acts 5:29 establishes the hierarchy: obeying God takes precedence over human rulers. Acts 5:32 ties obedience to God's gift of the Spirit, Acts 27:21 applies it to heeding Paul's practical counsel aboard ship, and Titus 3:1 extends it to civic submission toward governing authorities.

gloss_terse: Fifth; the ordinal number designating the fifth position in a sequence.
gloss_readable: A straightforward ordinal adjective from pente (five), used exclusively in Revelation within the New Testament. It marks the fifth seal (Rev 6:9), where martyred souls cry out from beneath the altar; the fifth trumpet/angel (Rev 9:1), unleashing the terrifying locust plague from the abyss; the fifth bowl of wrath (Rev 16:10), poured on the throne of the beast; and the fifth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem, identified as sardonyx (Rev 21:20). The translations are uniformly literal: Spanish quinto, French cinquieme, German fuenfte.

senses.1: The ordinal number fifth, designating the fifth item in a sequence. Every translation renders it with the standard ordinal (Spanish quinto, French cinquieme, German fuenfte). In Revelation, it structures the numbered series of divine judgments: the fifth seal reveals martyrs' souls (Rev 6:9), the fifth trumpet opens the abyss (Rev 9:1), the fifth bowl darkens the beast's kingdom (Rev 16:10), and the fifth foundation stone adorns the heavenly city (Rev 21:20).

gloss_terse: End, limit, boundary, extremity; the farthest point or ultimate conclusion of something.
gloss_readable: This neuter noun denotes an end, boundary, or outermost limit — whether spatial or conceptual. In Matthew 12:42 and Luke 11:31, the Queen of the South comes 'from the ends of the earth' to hear Solomon's wisdom, a vivid image of the remotest geographic boundary. Romans 10:18 quotes Psalm 19, declaring that the gospel message has gone out 'to the ends of the world.' Hebrews 6:16 shifts the sense from spatial to legal: an oath is 'an end' (a final settlement) of every dispute. Spanish confines/fin and German Ende both capture this dual range of spatial extremity and conclusive finality.

senses.1: An end, limit, boundary, or extremity — the farthest reach of a spatial expanse or the conclusive termination of a matter. The multilingual evidence splits revealingly: Spanish confines and French extremite emphasize spatial boundaries, while Spanish fin, French fin, and German Ende highlight conclusive finality. Matthew 12:42 and Luke 11:31 use the plural for the 'ends of the earth,' Romans 10:18 for the worldwide reach of divine speech, and Hebrews 6:16 applies the singular to an oath as the 'end' or final resolution of all dispute.
